title: Time-Series Splits & Backtesting
interviewAnswer: Random train/test splitting is usually wrong for forecasting because it leaks the future into the past. I split chronologically and evaluate with rolling or expanding-window backtests that mimic how the model will actually be used.
why: Forecast validation is easy to make unrealistically optimistic. A model should only use information that would have existed at the prediction timestamp.
intuition: Imagine standing at each historical date and pretending it is “today.” Train only on the past, forecast the next horizon, record the error, then move forward.
deepDive: Random cross-validation breaks temporal ordering. Use a final untouched future holdout for the last estimate, while rolling-origin validation compares models/hyperparameters. Feature engineering must also be point-in-time correct: rolling means, target encodings, and joins cannot peek ahead.
workedExample: For monthly demand, train Jan–Dec 2024 and validate Jan–Mar 2025; then train through Mar and validate Apr–Jun. Compare errors across windows instead of trusting one lucky split.
commonMistakes: Using random K-fold CV on dependent time-series observations.
Computing rolling features on the full dataset before splitting, which leaks future information.
followUps: When is random splitting acceptable for temporal data?
How do you choose expanding vs sliding windows?
production: Backtests should mirror prediction cadence, horizon, retraining frequency and data availability. Production feature pipelines need event-time/point-in-time semantics.
code:
# sklearn-style rolling evaluation
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
for train_idx, val_idx in tscv.split(X):
    X_train, X_val = X.iloc[train_idx], X.iloc[val_idx]
    y_train, y_val = y.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[val_idx]

lab.goal: Backtest without future leakage using expanding windows.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
y=np.arange(30)+np.sin(np.arange(30))
errors=[]
for cutoff in range(15,27,3):
    train=y[:cutoff]; val=y[cutoff:cutoff+3]
    pred=np.repeat(train[-1],len(val)) # naive baseline
    errors.append(mean_absolute_error(val,pred))
print(errors, np.mean(errors))
lab.verifyIt:
assert len(errors)==4
assert all(e>=0 for e in errors)
